P4g: Oventik itself was like something out of a dream. We played basketball outside with the Zapatista youth, and people gave us talks about their history and philosophy, which I translated for my friends because my Spanish was better. Visitors were coming from all around the world to learn, and to make the communities less easy to attack in silence.
P5g: I felt a deep spirituality from the Zapatistas. I also suspect there may be a private relationship with ayahuasca, but nobody told me that, and it's only my impression, not something to take as fact.
P7k2: The Zapatistas are also the closest whole example I found, because autonomy there isn't just a way of voting. They've built their own education and health care and justice, and their own collective production and political formation, and ways of teaching outsiders too, while coordinating beyond a single village.
P7k3: The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole example that I found, because autonomy there isn't just a way of voting. They've built their own education and health care and justice, and their own collective production and political formation, and ways of teaching outsiders too, while coordinating beyond a single village.
P13m1: Now, the Zapatistas also don't prove my whole economic path, from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money. Do their communities use collective work to support their schools and clinics, and their autonomous government and resistance? Yes. But they also sell products and trade, and they get outside support. So what do they show? That major necessities and public functions can move out of ordinary market purchase and be governed collectively. Outside help can make a community more capable, sure. But it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, if the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable.

P14z: For the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita, where outsiders lived with families and learned autonomy by taking part in day to day life. Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.
